claim: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is hypothesized to play a central role in the rapid stopping of movement in reaction to a stop signal.
source: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is hypothesized to play a central role in the rapid stopping of movement in reaction to a stop signal.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a hypothesis that motivates the study.

claim: Specific subsets of STN neurons have activity consistent with causal roles in reactive action stopping or switching.
source: We found that specific subsets of STN neurons have activity consistent with causal roles in reactive action stopping or switching.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by neuronal recording data presented in Figures 3-6.

claim: Neurons with stop-related or switch-related activity were strictly segregated to a ventromedial region of STN.
source: Importantly, these neurons were strictly segregated to a ventromedial region of STN.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical mapping data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neurons in other subdivisions of STN encoded task dimensions such as movement per se and proactive control.
source: Neurons in other subdivisions encoded task dimensions such as movement per se and proactive control.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Go/NoGo cells distributed throughout STN (Figure 8D) and Movement cells in different locations (Figure 4B).

claim: The involvement of STN in reactive control is restricted to its ventromedial portion.
source: We propose that the involvement of STN in reactive control is restricted to its ventromedial portion, further implicating this STN subdivision in impulse control disorders.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the anatomical distribution of Stop and Switch cells.

claim: Deficient forms of response inhibition are associated with many impulse control disorders.
source: Because deficient forms of response inhibition are associated with many impulse control disorders (Robbins et al., 2012; Bari and Robbins, 2013), a better understanding of the inhibition brain-network should help improve treatments for those patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stop-signal task performance is well explained by a race model in which the Go and Stop signals trigger independent processes that compete to be the first to finish.
source: Stop-signal task performance is well explained by a race model in which the Go and Stop signals trigger independent processes that compete to be the first to finish (Boucher et al., 2007; Logan et al., 1984; Verbruggen and Logan, 2009).
evidence: This is an established model in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Neuroimaging and lesion studies have posited a critical role for the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in stopping actions.
source: Neuroimaging and lesion studies have posited a critical role for the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in stopping actions (Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Aron et al., 2007; Li et al., 2008; Sharp et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous neuroimaging and lesion studies.

claim: STN lesions result in impulsive and perseverative behaviors.
source: Specifically, STN lesions result in impulsive and perseverative behaviors (Baunez et al., 1995; Wiener et al., 2008), with a reduced ability to suppress action in the stop-signal task (Eagle et al., 2008; Obeso et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to lesion studies.

claim: STN lesions result in a reduced ability to suppress action in the stop-signal task.
source: Specifically, STN lesions result in impulsive and perseverative behaviors (Baunez et al., 1995; Wiener et al., 2008), with a reduced ability to suppress action in the stop-signal task (Eagle et al., 2008; Obeso et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to lesion studies.

claim: In parkinsonian patients, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of STN has a variety of effects on the stopping of pre-planned or on-going actions.
source: In parkinsonian patients, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of STN has a variety of effects on the stopping of pre-planned or on-going actions (Mirabella et al., 2012; Obeso et al., 2013; Ray et al., 2009; Swann et al., 2011; van den Wildenberg et al., 2006), and beta frequency local field potentials are modulated by inhibitory processes (Alegre et al., 2013; Bastin et al., 2014; Benis et al., 2014; Kühn et al., 2004; Ray et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to DBS studies in Parkinson's patients.

claim: Beta frequency local field potentials in STN are modulated by inhibitory processes.
source: In parkinsonian patients, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of STN has a variety of effects on the stopping of pre-planned or on-going actions (Mirabella et al., 2012; Obeso et al., 2013; Ray et al., 2009; Swann et al., 2011; van den Wildenberg et al., 2006), and beta frequency local field potentials are modulated by inhibitory processes (Alegre et al., 2013; Bastin et al., 2014; Benis et al., 2014; Kühn et al., 2004; Ray et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: Recent single-unit recordings from rats showed that success or failure on the stop-signal task correlated with the timing of STN responses evoked by the stop-signal.
source: Recent single-unit recordings from rats showed that success or failure on the stop-signal task correlated with the timing of STN responses evoked by the stop-signal (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a rat electrophysiology study.

claim: Short-latency STN responses to stop cues were not selective to the Stop cue, but were also present for Go cues that prompted a switch in behavior.
source: These short-latency STN responses, for example, were not selective to the Stop cue (Mallet et al., 2016), but were also present for Go cues that prompted a switch in behavior (i.e. the selection and initiation of an alternate action).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A sub-population of STN neurons exhibit a change of activity when an animal is required to switch from an automatic action to one guided by sensory instructions.
source: Indeed, one non-human primate study reported that a sub-population of STN neurons exhibit a change of activity when an animal is required to switch from an automatic (i.e., pre-potent) action to one guided by sensory instructions (Isoda and Hikosaka, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a primate electrophysiology study.

claim: The posterior-dorsal-lateral STN is interconnected with a basal ganglia circuit devoted to skeletomotor function.
source: The posterior-dorsal-lateral STN is interconnected with a basal ganglia circuit devoted to skeletomotor function, whereas associative- and limbic-related territories are found in progressively more anterior, ventral and medial regions of the STN (Haynes and Haber, 2013; Mettler and Stern, 1962; Monakow et al., 1978; Shink et al., 1996; Wichmann et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Associative- and limbic-related territories are found in progressively more anterior, ventral and medial regions of the STN.
source: The posterior-dorsal-lateral STN is interconnected with a basal ganglia circuit devoted to skeletomotor function, whereas associative- and limbic-related territories are found in progressively more anterior, ventral and medial regions of the STN (Haynes and Haber, 2013; Mettler and Stern, 1962; Monakow et al., 1978; Shink et al., 1996; Wichmann et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Anterior ventromedial regions of the STN receive direct afferents from stop-associated regions of prefrontal cortex.
source: We predicted that activity correlated with movement inhibition would be concentrated in the anterior ventromedial regions of the STN known to receive direct afferents (Inase et al., 1999; Künzle, 1978) from stop-associated regions of prefrontal cortex (Aron et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Two monkeys were trained to perform a Go/NoGo-countermanding arm movement task.
source: Two monkeys (C and H) were trained to perform a Go/NoGo-countermanding arm movement task (Figure 1) that combines two paradigms commonly used to investigate the neuropsychology of inhibitory functions: the stop-signal task and the Go/NoGo task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, with reference to Figure 1 showing the task design.

claim: Median RTs for switch-stop trials in which the monkeys failed to suppress the response were faster than median RTs detected for go trials.
source: As is typical for stop-signal tasks (Scangos and Stuphorn, 2010; Mirabella et al., 2011), median RTs for switch-stop trials in which the monkeys failed to suppress the response (referred as stop-failure trials) were faster than median RTs detected for go trials (Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by statistical analysis and consistent with previous studies.

claim: The RT distributions for stop-failure trials were shifted to the left with respect to the RT distributions of go trials.
source: Figure 2 shows that the RT distributions calculated across sessions for stop-failure trials (C: median = 555 ± 64 ms; H: median = 502 ± 77 ms) were shifted to the left with respect to the RT distributions of go trials (C: median = 580 ± 58 ms; H: median = 516 ± 93 ms).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding shown in Figure 2 with specific RT values.

claim: The incidence of stop-failure trials increased as a function of the delay between the go trigger signal and the switch-signal.
source: As shown in Figure 2, the incidence of stop-failure trials increased (inhibition functions: linear regressions, p<0.05) as a function of the delay between the go trigger signal and the switch-signal (i.e., the switch-signal delay, SSD).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding shown in Figure 2 with statistical support.

claim: The average SSRT during the task was around 160 ms.
source: We calculated that the average SSRT during our task was around 160 ms (C: median = 169 ± 37 ms; H: median = 152 ± 47 ms).
evidence: This is a behavioral measure calculated from the data.

claim: The SSRTs had similar distributions for the two animals.
source: The SSRTs had similar distributions for the two animals (Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.14), but were slightly longer than those reported in earlier studies that used a manual stop-signal task [~140 ms (Scangos and Stuphorn, 2010);~150 ms (Mirabella et al., 2011)].
evidence: This is a comparison of behavioral measures between animals and with previous studies, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 167 neurons were recorded in the right STN while monkeys performed the Go/NoGo-countermanding task.
source: While the monkeys performed the Go/NoGo-countermanding task, we recorded single-unit activity from 167 neurons in the right STN (55 from monkey C; 112 from monkey H).
evidence: This is a description of the data collection.

claim: 63 neurons (38%) qualified as being involved in the stop process.
source: Of the 167 neurons recorded, 63 (38%) qualified as being involved in the stop process (see table in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: The average neural cancellation time was −55 ms before the SSRT.
source: The average neural cancellation time was −55 ms before the SSRT (C: median = −44 ± 32 ms; H: median = −58.5 ± 25 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: 78% (49 of 63) of STN neurons involved in the stop process were classified as Movement cells.
source: A large majority (78%; 49 of 63) of these STN neurons were classified as Movement cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neuronal classification.

claim: 22% (14 of 63) of STN neurons involved in the stop process responded to the switch-stop cue with a transient increase in firing rate suitable for an active role in the stop process.
source: Importantly, a second subset (22%; 14 of 63) of STN neurons responded to the switch-stop cue with a transient increase in firing rate suitable for an active role in the stop process.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neuronal classification.

claim: Switch-stop cells were found in only the most anterior, ventral, and medial portion of the STN.
source: Remarkably, Switch-stop cells were found in only the most anterior, ventral, and medial portion of the STN (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a key anatomical finding shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The same anatomic segregation of Switch-stop cells was observed in each animal considered independently.
source: The same anatomic segregation was observed in each animal considered independently.
evidence: This confirms the anatomical finding across both subjects.

claim: The anatomic 'hotspot' for Switch-stop cells is a territory well-described as receiving inputs from associative and limbic cortical areas.
source: This anatomic 'hotspot' is a territory well-described as receiving inputs from associative and limbic cortical areas (Haynes and Haber, 2013; Karachi et al., 2005) and as implicated in impulse control disorders (Baup et al., 2008; Mallet et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim connects the anatomical finding to previous literature on STN connectivity and function.

claim: Neuronal activities related to reward delivery or the occurrence of errors in task performance did not show a similar localization within the STN.
source: It is interesting to note that neuronal activities related to reward delivery or the occurrence of errors in task performance did not show a similar localization within the STN (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a control finding shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: No differences were found in the mean baseline firing rates of the different subtypes of STN neurons or between the two animals.
source: No differences were found in the mean baseline firing rates of the different subtypes of STN neurons or between the two animals (2-way ANOVA, F < 2.13 p>0.15).
evidence: This is a negative finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The inhibition of arm movement was accomplished by both a rapid relaxation of agonist muscles and a brief activation of antagonists.
source: The inhibition of arm movement was accomplished by both a rapid relaxation of agonist muscles and a brief activation of antagonists (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an EMG finding shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The cancellation times of Switch-stop and Movement cells preceded the majority of stop-related EMG activities.
source: Although we found that the cancellation times of Switch-stop and Movement cells preceded the majority of stop-related EMG activities (posterior deltoid = −30 ms, triceps = −51 ms, biceps = −94 ms; Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.05), no significant time lag was measured between STN signals and the changes of activity in the anterior deltoid (−10 ms; Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a comparison of neural and muscle timing, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: No significant time lag was measured between STN signals and the changes of activity in the anterior deltoid.
source: Although we found that the cancellation times of Switch-stop and Movement cells preceded the majority of stop-related EMG activities (posterior deltoid = −30 ms, triceps = −51 ms, biceps = −94 ms; Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.05), no significant time lag was measured between STN signals and the changes of activity in the anterior deltoid (−10 ms; Mann-Whitney U-test, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a timing comparison supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Of the 14 Switch-stop cells, 8 (57%) were classified as Stop cells.
source: Of the 14 Switch-stop cells, 8 (57%) were classified as Stop cells (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from further classification of Switch-stop cells.

claim: In 43% (6 of 14) of Switch-stop cells, responses were not selective for the condition when the cue signaled need for a rapid stop.
source: In the remainder (43%; 6 of 14), here termed Switch cells, responses were not selective for the condition when the cue signaled need for a rapid stop.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from further classification of Switch-stop cells.

claim: No difference was found in the neural cancellation times between Stop and Switch cells.
source: No difference was found in the neural cancellation times between Stop and Switch cells (Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.66).
evidence: This is a negative finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: No Switch-stop cells (0 of 14) had activity that encoded eye position or the timing of saccades.
source: Regression analyses found no Switch-stop cells (0 of 14; Permutation test, p>0.01) whose activity encoded eye position or the timing of saccades (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a negative finding from regression analysis, shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: 42 neurons (25%) exhibited short-latency responses to torque motor-induced movements.
source: Of the 167 neurons, 42 (25%) exhibited short-latency responses (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from proprioceptive testing.

claim: Torque responsive neurons were concentrated in the dorsal postero-lateral STN.
source: These 'Torque' responsive neurons were concentrated in the dorsal postero-lateral STN (Figure 7C), agreeing well with previous descriptions of the skeletomotor territory (Parent and Hazrati, 1995; Haynes and Haber, 2013).
evidence: This is an anatomical finding shown in Figure 7C and consistent with previous literature.

claim: 38% (16 of 42) of Torque cells were also Movement cells.
source: Many Torque cells (38%; 16 of 42) were also Movement cells (see above; Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about overlap between cell types.

claim: Only one Torque cell was categorized as a Switch cell (2%; 1 of 42).
source: In contrast, only one Torque cell was categorized as a Switch cell (2%; 1 of 42; Figure 7E–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about overlap between cell types.

claim: Torque cells were concentrated distant from the anterior ventromedial region where Stop and Switch cells were located.
source: Furthermore, Torque cells were concentrated distant from the anterior ventromedial region where Stop and Switch cells were located (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is an anatomical finding shown in Figure 7C.

claim: There was a significant prolongation of RTs in switch-go trials relative to those in go trials.
source: Evidence that the NoGo instruction induced a proactive behavioral set to not respond included a significant prolongation of RTs in switch-go trials relative to those in go trials (Mann-Whitney U-test, p<0.001; see preparation cost in Figure 8—figure supplement 1), which did not differ between monkeys (Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.82).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Go neurons (37%; 61 of 167) showed elevated tonic firing during the instructed delay period of go trials relative to that of no-go trials.
source: Go neurons (37%; 61 of 167) showed elevated tonic firing during the instructed delay period of go trials relative to that of no-go trials (Figure 8C) and thus were considered unlikely to play an important role in proactive impulse control.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from neuronal classification.

claim: NoGo cells (25%; 41 of 167) showed elevated delay period activity during no-go trials.
source: NoGo cells (25%; 41 of 167) showed elevated delay period activity during no-go trials.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from neuronal classification.

claim: Neither Go nor NoGo cell categories showed evidence of anatomic clustering within the STN.
source: Neither category showed evidence of anatomic clustering within the STN (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is an anatomical finding shown in Figure 8D.

claim: No obvious interaction was found between the categories of neurons associated with reactive and proactive control.
source: We found no obvious interaction between the categories of neurons associated with reactive and proactive control (χ2 test, χ2 = 1.75, p=0.42).
evidence: This is a negative finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Roughly equal proportions of Switch-stop cells were categorized as Go cells (4 of 14) and NoGo cells (5 of 14).
source: Roughly equal proportions of Switch-stop cells were categorized as Go cells (4 of 14) and NoGo cells (5 of 14), while the remainder showed no preferential activity during the instructed delay period (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about overlap between cell types.

claim: Two distinct mechanisms support reactive and proactive modes of action control.
source: Together, these results suggest that two distinct mechanisms support reactive and proactive modes of action control.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of interaction between reactive and proactive cell types.

claim: The present results provide the first evidence for a selective encoding of stopping at the cellular level in the healthy primate STN.
source: To our knowledge, these results provide the first evidence for a selective encoding of stopping at the cellular level in the healthy primate STN.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: More than one-third of STN neurons met the temporal criterion for involvement in stopping (neural cancellation time within SSRT).
source: More than one-third of our STN neurons met this temporal criterion (Figures 3–4).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the neuronal data.

claim: The most common response pattern among STN neurons meeting the temporal criterion was a movement-related activation that decayed rapidly in response to the stop-signal.
source: Among those cells, the most common response pattern was a movement-related activation that decayed rapidly in response to the stop-signal, similar to the activity observed in agonist muscles (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the most common neuronal response pattern.

claim: The second response pattern consisted of a phasic increase in discharge in response to the stop-signal.
source: Notably, the second response pattern consisted of a phasic increase in discharge in response to the stop-signal.
evidence: This is a description of the second neuronal response pattern.

claim: The mean neural cancellation time for Movement cells was slightly earlier than that for Stop cells.
source: We found, however, that the mean neural cancellation time for Movement cells was slightly earlier than that for Stop cells.
evidence: This is a timing comparison between cell types.

claim: Stop-related activity preceded the earliest stop-related truncation of EMG activity by a mere 10 ms.
source: Moreover, Stop-related activity preceded the earliest stop-related truncation of EMG activity by a mere 10 ms.
evidence: This is a timing comparison between neural and muscle activity.

claim: The STN is part of the network in which visual attention and the salience of events are implemented.
source: Indeed, the STN is part of the network in which visual attention and the salience of events are implemented (Baunez and Robbins, 1997; Baunez et al., 2007; Bočková et al., 2011; Schmalbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 43% of cells with short-latency stop responses responded similarly or more strongly with sudden action initiation in switch-go trials.
source: Although standard criteria would have classified all as playing an active role in stopping, 43% of cells with short-latency stop responses responded similarly or more strongly with sudden action initiation in switch-go trials.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparison of switch-stop and switch-go trials.

claim: Stop and Switch cells did not overlap, categorically or anatomically, with the STN neurons most likely to be involved directly in the activation of antagonist muscles.
source: These cells did not overlap, categorically or anatomically, with the STN neurons most likely to be involved directly in the activation of antagonist muscles, namely those responsive to proprioceptive stimulation and concentrated in the skeletomotor territory of the STN (Nambu et al., 2002; Parent and Hazrati, 1995; Baron et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding about the lack of overlap between cell types, with reference to previous literature on STN organization.

claim: Schmidt et al. described a population of STN neurons in the rat that responded at short-latency to a Stop cue.
source: Schmidt et al. (2013) described a population of STN neurons in the rat that responded at short-latency to a Stop cue.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study.

claim: In the Schmidt et al. study, STN neurons also responded at roughly equal latency and magnitude to the Go cue.
source: Notably, unlike the present study, those neurons also responded at roughly equal latency and magnitude to the Go cue, which was presented on all trials (Mallet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study, contrasting with the present results.

claim: Benis et al. described distinct sub-populations of STN neurons that responded selectively and at short latency to Stop and Go task signals in human subjects undergoing DBS surgery.
source: In a recent study in human subjects undergoing DBS surgery for Parkinson's disease, Benis et al. (2016) described distinct sub-populations of STN neurons that responded selectively and at short latency to Stop and Go task signals, similar to our findings.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study that are consistent with the present results.

claim: Isoda and Hikosaka found a distinct sub-population of STN neurons that responded selectively and at short latency to an unexpected switch stimulus in macaques.
source: Isoda and Hikosaka (2008) recorded from the macaque STN during a task that required animals to switch behaviors between familiar and unexpected oculomotor responses, somewhat similar to our switch-go type trials. Like us, they found a distinct sub-population of STN neurons that responded selectively and at short latency to the unexpected switch stimulus.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study that are consistent with the present results.

claim: No previous study dissociated STN activities related to reactive stopping, reactive switching and proactive (NoGo) response control.
source: No previous study, however, dissociated STN activities related to reactive stopping, reactive switching and proactive (NoGo) response control, tested for potential overlap between stop-related activity and skeletomotor responsiveness, or addressed whether stop-related activity is concentrated in a sub-region of the STN.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the present study compared to previous work.

claim: Similar movement- and stop-related response patterns have been found in frontal eye cortex and superior colliculus of macaques performing an eye movement countermanding task.
source: Finally, similar movement- and stop-related response patterns have been found in frontal eye cortex and superior colliculus of macaques performing an eye movement countermanding task (Schall and Godlove, 2012; Hanes et al., 1998; Paré and Hanes, 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings in other brain areas, supported by citations.

claim: The STN includes an oculomotor territory.
source: Although the STN includes an oculomotor territory (Matsumura et al., 1992), we found no evidence that the Stop-related activity identified here actually reflected movements of the eyes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement about STN organization supported by citation, followed by a negative finding from the present study.

claim: Fully a quarter of STN neurons exhibited sustained activity preferentially after a NoGo cue.
source: Fully a quarter of STN neurons exhibited sustained activity preferentially after a NoGo cue (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about NoGo-related activity.

claim: NoGo cells were not confined to a particular territory of the STN.
source: These cells were not confined to a particular territory of the STN, a result that contrasted sharply with the anatomically-restricted location of stop cells.
evidence: This is an anatomical finding contrasting NoGo cells with Stop cells.

claim: The distribution of NoGo cells throughout the STN implies that many functional sub-circuits through the STN are activated during this behavior.
source: The distribution of NoGo cells throughout the STN implies that many functional sub-circuits through the STN are activated during this behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anatomical distribution of NoGo cells.

claim: Previous studies have implicated the striatum and the striato-pallidal-STN 'indirect' pathway in proactive control.
source: Previous studies have implicated the striatum and the striato-pallidal-STN 'indirect' pathway in proactive control (Casey et al., 1997; Kelly et al., 2004; Smittenaar et al., 2013; Vink et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: Proactive and reactive movement suppressions involve categorically different neural mechanisms.
source: Although the present results do not address that possibility, they do argue that proactive and reactive movement suppressions involve categorically different neural mechanisms.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of overlap between Stop/Switch cells and NoGo cells.

claim: The presence of NoGo activity in a single-unit had no predictive power over whether that unit also responded preferentially to switch-stop or switch-go signals.
source: Not only were Stop and NoGo activities distributed differently within the STN, but the presence of NoGo activity in a single-unit had no predictive power over whether that unit also responded preferentially to switch-stop or switch-go signals (Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding about the independence of reactive and proactive cell types.

claim: The STN receives topographically-organized glutamatergic inputs from most regions of the frontal cortex.
source: The STN receives topographically-organized glutamatergic inputs from most regions of the frontal cortex (Nambu et al., 2002; Haynes and Haber, 2013; Monakow et al., 1978).
evidence: This is a statement about STN connectivity supported by citations.

claim: The inferior frontal cortex (IFC) has been linked closely to reactive stopping based on lesion and stimulation studies.
source: Among these, the inferior frontal cortex (IFC; potential homologue in macaques: area 45) has been linked closely to reactive stopping based on lesion (Aron et al., 2003; Swick et al., 2008) and stimulation (Verbruggen et al., 2010; Wessel et al., 2013) studies.
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings about IFC function, supported by citations.

claim: Most prefrontal areas project to ventral and medial portions of the STN that encompass the regions where Stop and Switch cells were located.
source: Although the specific topography of the IFC–to–STN projection has yet to be determined, tract-tracing studies indicate that most prefrontal areas [i.e., ventromedial, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate and dorsal prefrontal cortices (Haynes and Haber, 2013)] project to ventral and medial portions of the STN that encompass the regions where Stop and Switch cells were located.
evidence: This is a statement about STN connectivity based on previous tract-tracing studies, related to the present anatomical findings.

claim: The ventromedial portion of STN receives strong GABAergic inputs from the rostral-medial external pallidum and ventral pallidum.
source: This portion of the STN also receives strong GABAergic inputs from the rostral-medial external pallidum (part of the BG associative circuit) and ventral pallidum (of the BG limbic circuit) (Haynes and Haber, 2013; Shink et al., 1996; Karachi et al., 2005), and additional glutamatergic inputs from the parafascicular nucleus of the thalamus, also a limbic circuit-connected nucleus (Sadikot et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a statement about STN connectivity supported by citations.

claim: The ventromedial region of STN contained few cells with Movement-like activity.
source: Consistent with its afferent connectivity, this ventromedial region contained few cells with Movement-like activity (Figure 4B), making it unlikely that Stop and Go processes are compared locally within the ventromedial STN.
evidence: This is an anatomical finding with an interpretation about local processing.

claim: A commonly accepted model states that the first efferent step from the STN is a highly divergent projection to the output nuclei of the BG.
source: A commonly accepted model states that the first efferent step from the STN is a highly divergent projection to the output nuclei of the BG [i.e., internal pallidum (GPi) and SNr] (Aron, 2011; Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of a prevailing model, supported by citations.

claim: Divergence in the STN-GPi/SNr pathway is said to be crucial for the broadcast of stop-related activity from the associative/limbic territory of the STN to GABAergic neurons in the skeletomotor and oculomotor territories of GPi and SNr.
source: Divergence in this pathway is said to be crucial for the broadcast of stop-related activity from the associative/limbic territory of the STN to GABAergic neurons in the skeletomotor and oculomotor territories of GPi and SNr, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical mechanism in the prevailing model.

claim: Limited evidence supports divergence in the STN-GPi/SNr pathway.
source: Limited evidence supports divergence in the STN-GPi/SNr pathway, however (Hazrati and Parent, 1992), while multiple lines of evidence indicate instead that this axonal projection is highly specific and topographically organized (Shink et al., 1996; Smith et al., 1998; Kolomiets et al., 2001; Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of the prevailing model, supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Multiple lines of evidence indicate that the STN-GPi/SNr axonal projection is highly specific and topographically organized.
source: Limited evidence supports divergence in the STN-GPi/SNr pathway, however (Hazrati and Parent, 1992), while multiple lines of evidence indicate instead that this axonal projection is highly specific and topographically organized (Shink et al., 1996; Smith et al., 1998; Kolomiets et al., 2001; Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about STN connectivity supported by multiple citations.

claim: Potential alternative pathways for STN stop signals include the direct STN projection to the tegmental pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) and the disynaptic STN-GPi/SNr-PPN pathway.
source: Potential alternative pathways include the direct STN projection to the tegmental pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) (Shink et al., 1996; Hazrati and Parent, 1992; Parent and Smith, 1987; Nakano et al., 1990; Smith et al., 1990) as well as the disynaptic STN-GPi/SNr-PPN pathway.
evidence: This is a proposal for alternative pathways, supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Selective activation of cholinergic neurons of the ventral PPN triggers a short-latency and wide-spread inhibition of motor output.
source: It is interesting to note in this respect that selective activation of cholinergic neurons of the ventral PPN triggers a short-latency and wide-spread inhibition of motor output (Takakusaki et al., 1993; Takakusaki et al., 2016; Kohyama et al., 1998) in addition to a range of alerting and behavior-modulating functions (Mena-Segovia et al., 2004; Gut and Winn, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about PPN function supported by citations, relevant to the proposed alternative pathway.

claim: It is quite likely that reactive stopping depends on a cascade of movement-suppressive processes and multiple brain pathways.
source: And, as mentioned in the Introduction, it is quite likely that reactive stopping such as that studied here depends on a cascade of movement-suppressive processes and multiple brain pathways (Pouget et al., 2017; Schmidt and Berke, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of stopping mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: The STN influences motor control centers primarily via direct excitation of the GABAergic output neurons of the BG.
source: Making sense of this type of activity is complicated by the widely-held view that the STN influences motor control centers primarily via direct excitation of the GABAergic output neurons of the BG (in GPi and SNr) (Nambu et al., 2002; Wichmann et al., 1994; Hamada and DeLong, 1992).
evidence: This is a description of a prevailing view about STN function, supported by citations.

claim: One recently-proposed solution is that another STN efferent pathway, which inhibits BG output neurons via a disynaptic pathway through the external pallidum (GPe), may dominate function of the circuit in certain behavioral contexts.
source: One recently-proposed solution is that another STN efferent pathway, which inhibits BG output neurons via a disynaptic pathway through the external pallidum (GPe), may dominate function of the circuit in certain behavioral contexts (Jantz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of a recently proposed alternative model, supported by citation.

claim: The present results concur in general terms with existing lines of evidence that implicate the ventromedial STN in various clinical disorders of inhibitory control.
source: The present results concur in general terms with existing lines of evidence that implicate the ventromedial STN in various clinical disorders of inhibitory control.
evidence: This is a statement connecting the present findings to clinical literature.

claim: DBS in the ventral STN produces greater effects on inhibitory control behaviors than does stimulation in the dorsal STN.
source: Case studies have shown that DBS in the ventral STN produces greater effects on inhibitory control behaviors than does stimulation in the dorsal STN (Greenhouse et al., 2013; Hershey et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a summary of clinical findings, supported by citations.

claim: The ventromedial STN is a current target for STN-DBS to treat severe obsessive compulsive disorder.
source: In fact, this anatomic location is a current target for STN-DBS to treat severe obsessive compulsive disorder (Mallet et al., 2008), which is considered a disorder of inhibitory control.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical practice, supported by citation.

claim: Local micro-infusions of bicuculline (a GABA antagonist) only into the ventromedial part of the STN induced stereotypies and hyperactive behaviors.
source: And local micro-infusions of bicuculline (a GABA antagonist) only into that part of the STN induced stereotypies and hyperactive behaviors (Karachi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of a pharmacological study, supported by citation.

claim: The present study is the first to show that single unit encoding of reactive stopping is restricted to the anterior ventromedial STN.
source: The present study is the first to show that single unit encoding of reactive stopping also is restricted to the anterior ventromedial STN.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the present findings.

claim: Activity related to rapid response switching (Switch cells) was also confined to the same anatomic hotspot as Stop cells.
source: It is interesting to note that activity related to rapid response switching (i.e., Switch cells) was also confined to the same anatomic hotspot (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is an anatomical finding shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Pittsburgh (protocol number: 12111162).
source: Procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Pittsburgh (protocol number: 12111162) and complied with the Public Health Service Policy on the humane care and use of laboratory animals (amended 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.
